facts.statement: Gorgosaurus lived in western North America during the Late Cretaceous Period (Campanian) between approximately 76.5 and 73 million years ago.
facts.quote: Gorgosaurus ( ; ) is a genus of tyrannosaurid theropod dinosaur that lived in western North America during the Late Cretaceous Period (Campanian), between about 76.5 and 73 million years ago.

facts.statement: Fossil remains of Gorgosaurus have been found in Western Canada and the U.S. state of Montana.
facts.quote: Fossil remains have been found in Western Canada as well as the U.S. state of Montana.

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus possessed dozens of large, sharp teeth in its jaws and small, two-fingered forelimbs.
facts.quote: Dozens of large, sharp teeth lined its jaws, while its two-fingered forelimbs were comparatively small.

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus inhabited a lush floodplain environment located along the edge of an inland sea.
facts.quote: Gorgosaurus lived in a lush floodplain environment along the edge of an inland sea.

facts.statement: As an apex predator, Gorgosaurus preyed on abundant ceratopsids and hadrosaurs.
facts.quote: It was an apex predator, preying upon abundant ceratopsids and hadrosaurs.

facts.statement: In some areas, Gorgosaurus coexisted with the tyrannosaurid Daspletosaurus.
facts.quote: In some areas, Gorgosaurus coexisted with another tyrannosaurid, Daspletosaurus.

facts.statement: The species Gorgosaurus libratus was first described by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.
facts.quote: Gorgosaurus libratus was first described by Lawrence Lambe in 1914.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen (NMC 2120) of Gorgosaurus libratus, a nearly complete skeleton with a skull, was discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg.
facts.quote: The holotype of Gorgosaurus libratus (NMC 2120) is a nearly complete skeleton associated with a skull, discovered in 1913 by Charles M. Sternberg.

facts.statement: The holotype was found in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta and is now housed in the Canadian Museum of Nature in Ottawa.
facts.quote: It was found in the Dinosaur Park Formation of Alberta and is housed in the Canadian Museum of Nature in Ottawa.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen was the first tyrannosaurid skeleton ever found with a complete hand.
facts.quote: This specimen was the first tyrannosaurid found with a complete hand.

facts.statement: Matthew and Brown described four Gorgosaurus specimens collected by prospectors in 1923.
facts.quote: Matthew and Brown described four of these specimens in 1923.

facts.statement: Matthew and Brown described a fifth skeleton (AMNH 5664) that Charles H. Sternberg collected in 1917 and sold to the American Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: Matthew and Brown also described a fifth skeleton (AMNH 5664), which Charles H. Sternberg had collected in 1917 and sold to their museum.

facts.statement: A Montana specimen (TCMI 2001.89.1) housed in the Children's Museum of Indianapolis shows severe pathologies, including healed fractures, jaw infection causing tooth loss, and a possible brain tumor.
facts.quote: One specimen from Montana (TCMI 2001.89.1), housed in the Children's Museum of Indianapolis, shows evidence of severe pathologies, including healed leg, rib, and vertebral fractures, osteomyelitis (infection) at the tip of the lower jaw resulting in permanent tooth loss, and possibly a brain tumor.

facts.statement: Some experts debate whether Gorgosaurus libratus is a distinct species or merely a synonym of the genus Albertosaurus.
facts.quote: Some experts consider G. libratus to be a species of Albertosaurus; this would make Gorgosaurus a junior synonym of that genus.

facts.statement: In 1856, Joseph Leidy named the genus Deinodon based on two large, robust tyrannosaurid teeth found in Montana, without knowing the animal's full appearance.
facts.quote: In 1856, Joseph Leidy described two tyrannosaurid premaxillary teeth from Montana. Although there was no indication of what the animal looked like, the teeth were large and robust, and Leidy gave them the name Deinodon.

facts.statement: Because tyrannosaurid teeth are extremely uniform, it cannot be confirmed with certainty whether the teeth of Deinodon belong to Gorgosaurus.
facts.quote: Although Deinodon teeth are very similar to those of Gorgosaurus, tyrannosaurid teeth are extremely uniform, so it cannot be said for certain which animal they belonged to.

facts.statement: Several tyrannosaurid skeletons from Montana formations are thought to belong to Gorgosaurus, but it is uncertain if they represent G. libratus or a new species.
facts.quote: Several tyrannosaurid skeletons from the Two Medicine Formation and Judith River Formation of Montana probably belong to Gorgosaurus, although it remains uncertain whether they belong to G. libratus or a new species.

facts.statement: Charles Whitney Gilmore named a small tyrannosaurid skull from Montana Gorgosaurus lancensis in 1946.
facts.quote: A complete skull of a small tyrannosaurid (CMNH 7541), found in the younger, late Maastrichtian-age Hell Creek Formation of Montana, was named Gorgosaurus lancensis by Charles Whitney Gilmore in 1946.

facts.statement: The specimen previously named Gorgosaurus lancensis was renamed Nanotyrannus by Bob Bakker and colleagues in 1988.
facts.quote: This specimen was renamed Nanotyrannus by Bob Bakker and colleagues in 1988.

facts.statement: Evgeny Maleev named two small tyrannosaurid specimens from Mongolia Gorgosaurus lancinator and Gorgosaurus novojilovi in 1955.
facts.quote: Evgeny Maleev created the names Gorgosaurus lancinator and Gorgosaurus novojilovi for two small tyrannosaurid specimens (PIN 553-1 and PIN 552–2) from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia in 1955.

facts.statement: Kenneth Carpenter renamed one of Maleev's specimens in 1992, but both are now considered to be juvenile Tarbosaurus bataar.
facts.quote: Kenneth Carpenter renamed the smaller specimen Maleevosaurus novojilovi in 1992, but both are now considered juveniles of Tarbosaurus bataar.

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus are extremely similar, with distinctions found mainly in subtle differences in their teeth and skull bones.
facts.quote: Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus are extremely similar, distinguished mainly by subtle differences in the teeth and skull bones.

facts.statement: Despite being roughly the same size as Daspletosaurus, there is evidence of niche differentiation between the two tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Although these animals were roughly the same size, there is some evidence of niche differentiation between the two.

facts.statement: Adult Gorgosaurus measured 8 to 9 meters in length and weighed between 2 and 3 metric tons.
facts.quote: Adults reached 8 to 9 m in length from snout to tail, and weighed 2 - 3 MT in body mass.

facts.statement: The largest known Gorgosaurus skull measured 99 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The largest known skull measures 99 cm long, just slightly smaller than that of Daspletosaurus.

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus had a circular eye socket, unlike the oval or keyhole-shaped sockets of other tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: The eye socket was circular rather than oval or keyhole-shaped as in other tyrannosaurid genera.

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus possessed 26 to 30 maxillary teeth and 30 to 34 dentary teeth in addition to its eight premaxillary teeth.
facts.quote: Along with the eight premaxillary teeth, Gorgosaurus had 26 to 30 maxillary teeth and 30 to 34 teeth in the dentary bones of the lower jaw.

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus forelimbs had two functional digits, though a vestigial third metacarpal is present in some specimens.
facts.quote: The forelimbs had only two digits, although a third metacarpal is known in some specimens, the vestigial remains of the third digit seen in other theropods.

facts.statement: The largest known Gorgosaurus femur measured 105 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The largest known Gorgosaurus femur measured 105 cm long.

facts.statement: Isolated patches of Gorgosaurus skin show scales that are denser and larger than those on the holotype but still relatively fine, comparable to a Gila monster's scales.
facts.quote: Other patches of isolated Gorgosaurus skin shows denser, and larger though still relatively fine scales (smaller than hadrosaurid scales and approximately as fine as a Gila monster's).

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus is sometimes considered a junior synonym of Albertosaurus because Albertosaurus was named first.
facts.quote: Albertosaurus was named first, so by convention it is given priority over the name Gorgosaurus, which is sometimes considered its junior synonym.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus should be maintained as separate genera or combined into one.
facts.quote: Other experts maintain the two genera as separate.

facts.statement: A 2023 report described a juvenile Gorgosaurus fossil containing the intact remains of two juvenile Citipes in its stomach.
facts.quote: In 2023, a juvenile Gorgosaurus (TMP 2009.12.14) with its in situ stomach contents containing two Citipes juveniles about a year old intact was reported from the Dinosaur Park Formation.

facts.statement: The presence of only hindlimb and tail vertebrae in the stomach suggests juvenile Gorgosaurus preferentially consumed the muscular hindlimbs of its prey.
facts.quote: Only the remains of the hindlimbs and caudal vertebrae of juvenile Citipes were present in the tyrannosaurid's stomach cavity, suggesting that a juvenile Gorgosaurus may have had preferential consumption of the muscular hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Gorgosaurus spent up to half of its life in a juvenile phase before reaching near-maximum size in just a few years.
facts.quote: Gorgosaurus spent as much as half its life in the juvenile phase before ballooning up to near-maximum size in only a few years

facts.statement: Researchers estimate that Gorgosaurus underwent a dietary shift when its lower jaw reached a length of 58 cm.
facts.quote: It is estimated that an ontogenetic dietary shift of Gorgosaurus and Albertosaurus occurs when the mandibular length reaches 58 cm

facts.statement: Based on body size estimates, researchers suggest a mature female tyrannosaurid like Gorgosaurus might have laid clutches weighing 54-60 kg, corresponding to 21-32 eggs.
facts.quote: On the basis of these body size estimates, Longrich et al. (2026) suggested that the clutch of the confirmed, reproductively mature female T. rex (MOR 1125) would have weighed at least 54 - 60 kg which would possibly correspond to 21-32 eggs

facts.statement: The holotype of Gorgosaurus libratus (NMC 2120) shows healed fractures on the 13th and 14th gastralia, the left fibula, and the third right dorsal rib.
facts.quote: Several pathologies have been documented in the Gorgosaurus libratus holotype, NMC 2120. These include the third right dorsal rib, as well as healed fractures on the 13th and 14th gastralia and left fibula

facts.statement: A Gorgosaurus specimen (TMP94.12.602) bears a 10 cm longitudinal fracture in the middle of its right fibula.
facts.quote: Another specimen cataloged as TMP94.12.602 bears multiple pathologies. A 10 cm longitudinal fracture is present in the middle of the right fibula's shaft

facts.statement: Some Gorgosaurus specimens show healed bite wounds on the face that indicate the animal survived the injury.
facts.quote: Lesions from a bite received to the face were present and showed evidence that the wounds were healing before the animal died

facts.statement: A juvenile skull with tyrannosaur bite marks, initially thought to be Daspletosaurus, was later reclassified as Gorgosaurus libratus.
facts.quote: Specimen TMP 1994.143.1, a juvenile skull from the Dinosaur Park Formation with several tyrannosaur bite marks, was previously believed to be Daspletosaurus sp. but was later assigned to Gorgosaurus libratus

facts.statement: A Gorgosaurus right maxilla (TMP 2017.012.0002) displays five raised scars from healed injuries caused by face-biting from other Gorgosaurus.
facts.quote: TMP 2017.012.0002 is a Gorgosaurus right maxilla with five raised scars; healed injuries from face biting by conspecifics

facts.statement: Ralph Molnar speculated that a mushroom-shaped growth on a Gorgosaurus toe bone might be the same pathology found in an unidentified ornithomimid.
facts.quote: Ralph Molnar has speculated that this may be the same kind of pathology afflicting an unidentified ornithomimid discovered with a similar mushroom shaped growth on a toe bone

facts.statement: The youngest known Gorgosaurus fossil in Canada comes from the Wapiti Formation and is dated to approximately 73.77 million years ago.
facts.quote: The geologically youngest known Gorgosaurus fossil in Canada is known from the Wapiti Formation of British Columbia, most likely from either Unit 2 or 3 which is dated to the late Campanian, approximately 73.77 ± 1.46 million years ago.
